memo.intro: First-look memo as of 2026-11-03. Public data only. Every factual sentence links to its source; a separate verifier removed unsupported claims. Paragraphs marked Analysis are the research agent's judgment, not cited fact.

sentences.text: formiat/px4-ros2-drone-nav is a C++ repository described as autonomous UAV navigation in GNSS-denied indoor spaces with no prior map.
sentences.note: Language C++ and the description text match the source.

sentences.text: The stack combines stereo VIO (MSCKF), lidar-inertial odometry with map-based relocalization, 3D occupancy mapping, D* Lite path planning and GPU MPPI obstacle avoidance, running on PX4, ROS 2 and Gazebo SITL.
sentences.note: Description lists all components and PX4 + ROS 2 + Gazebo SITL.

sentences.text: formiat/drone-swarm-lab is a Rust research playground for drone swarm mission simulation, allocation strategies, benchmarks, and replay analysis.
sentences.note: Repo name, Rust and description match, but source says nothing about the 'same account' hosting it beyond the formiat prefix; that is minor, though 'account' is inferred from the full_name formiat/drone-swarm-lab, which does match the owner. Actually fully stated by the full_name.

sentences.text: The evidence names no founders or employees, so the team's background, size and robotics experience are unknown.
The px4-ros2-drone-nav tree at commit e53dc51 holds 1194 files, of which 992 are code files, and it lists environment fixtures named compact_3d_passage and dark_hall plus a fog media tool.
sentences.note: 1194 files, 992 code files, commit e53dc51, fixtures compact_3d_passage and dark_hall, and tools/media/fog all listed.

sentences.text: The drone-swarm-lab tree at commit 24f3bdc holds 584 files and lists results folders for PX4 SITL, PX4 SIH multi-agent runs, failure reallocation and packet-loss degradation coverage.
sentences.note: 584 files at 24f3bdc; results paths for px4_sitl, multi_agent_px4_sih, failure_reallocation and degradation_coverage_packet_loss are listed.

sentences.text: The hard problem is state estimation that stays consistent in feature-poor, dark or dusty indoor spaces, where visual features vanish and lidar can degenerate in long corridors.

Pairing a stereo MSCKF with lidar-inertial odometry is a sensible redundancy choice, but both components are well-known public algorithms, so the novelty is likely in integration and testing rather than in the core methods.
Running MPPI on a GPU for obstacle avoidance is a reasonable fit for cluttered 3D space, but it forces an onboard GPU with its weight and power cost, which strains small airframes.
The fog and dark-hall fixtures suggest the author is testing degraded perception, yet the evidence shows only simulation-style fixtures and no flight data on real hardware.
Open-source PX4 and ROS 2 tooling plus Gazebo SITL now let a small team build and test a full GNSS-denied autonomy stack in simulation without owning a fleet.

Interest in GNSS-denied flight has grown with electronic warfare in current conflicts and with demand for inspection in mines, tunnels and buildings, which pushes buyers toward vision and lidar navigation.
The repository's recent traction, with 9 releases between 2026-08-15 and 2026-10-31, shows an active build phase that matches this demand window.
The likely buyers are defense and public-safety units needing indoor reconnaissance, plus industrial operators inspecting mines, tunnels, tanks and warehouses.
Most of those buyers purchase a complete airframe or a flight-controller integration rather than a navigation library, so a software-only vendor must find an OEM or integrator partner.
The repository has a stated link to DARPA SubT Urban through its topics, which signals a target of subterranean and urban autonomy.

Technical risk: results shown only in Gazebo SITL may not survive real sensor noise, vibration, timing jitter and lighting, so state estimation drift could break navigation on actual flights.
Commercial risk: the code is public, so a defense or inspection buyer can use it for free and pay only an integrator, leaving little to charge for unless there is a hardened, supported product.
Competition risk: established players in GNSS-denied drone autonomy and large open-source communities can match a feature set quickly, and a single visible author has little to protect against that.
Team risk: a repository with this much code created in a few months may be one person or heavily AI-assisted, which raises doubts about maintainability and bus factor.
Attention risk: the fork cluster in mid-September and the star bursts may reflect a social media post rather than lasting users, since only one outside issue exists.
The public record does not say who the founders are, whether a company exists, or whether anyone is funding the work.
It does not show any real-hardware flight, any payload and compute specification, or any measured drift and success rates.
It does not show customers, pilots or a business model, or how the swarm lab relates to the navigation stack.
The license terms are present as a file but their effect on commercial use is not stated in the evidence.

founder_call_questions: Who is on the team, and how much of the code was written by you versus generated with AI tools?
Have you flown this stack on real hardware, and what airframe, sensors and compute did you use?
What is the measured drift and mission success rate in dark, foggy or featureless corridors, in real flight and in simulation?
How does the MSCKF and lidar-inertial odometry fusion behave when one sensor degrades, and how do you detect it?
What GPU does the MPPI planner need, and what is the power and weight cost on a small drone?
Which license applies to px4-ros2-drone-nav, and how do you plan to make money if the code stays open?
Who has asked for this, and who are the people behind the forks and the one outside issue?
How does drone-swarm-lab relate to the navigation stack, and is swarming part of the product?
Which customer segment would you sell to first, and would you sell software, a module or a full vehicle?
What did you learn from DARPA SubT Urban benchmarks, and how do your results compare with published entries?
